title: Here Documents and Here Strings
summary: Write blocks of text into commands and files with heredocs, feed one string to a command with a here string, and redirect a whole group of commands at once.
intro: Scripts often need to write more than one line: a usage message, a config file, a report. A here document feeds a block of text to a command's stdin, and a here string does the same for a single string. Every program in this lesson runs in a fresh folder holding the scriptbox files, such as `hosts.txt` and `build/VERSION`, which the Files strip lists.

steps.title: Here documents
steps.body:
A here document, or heredoc, feeds the lines between `<<EOF` and a line holding just `EOF` to a command's stdin. Bash expands variables and `$(...)` inside it first, as it does in double quotes:

```bash
name="Ada"
cat <<EOF
Hello, $name.
You are logged in as $(whoami).
EOF
```

Quote the word, as in `<<'EOF'`, and nothing expands. That's what you want when the text is itself a script. In an unquoted heredoc, `\$` gives a literal dollar sign.

```bash
cat <<'EOF'
echo "Hello, $USER"
EOF
```

To write a file, redirect the command: `cat > site.conf <<EOF`. `EOF` is only a habit: any word works. The closing line must hold that word alone, with nothing before or after it. With `<<-EOF`, Bash removes leading tabs (not spaces) from every line, so a heredoc can be indented inside an `if` or a function.

examples.title: A usage message
examples.prompt: Print a script's usage message, with the version read from `build/VERSION` and the script's own name from `$0`.
examples.code:
version="$(< build/VERSION)"

cat <<EOF
deploy $version: copy the build to every host

Usage: $0 [--dry-run] [HOST...]
With no HOST, it deploys to the $(wc -l < hosts.txt) hosts in hosts.txt.
EOF
examples.output:
deploy 1.4.2: copy the build to every host

Usage: main.sh [--dry-run] [HOST...]
With no HOST, it deploys to the 5 hosts in hosts.txt.
examples.explanation: `cat` prints its stdin, and the heredoc is its stdin. Before `cat` sees the text, Bash fills in `$version`, `$0`, and the `$(wc -l < hosts.txt)` command. `$0` is the name the script was started as, `main.sh` here. The blank line stays, because a heredoc keeps every line exactly as written up to the closing `EOF`. That's why usage messages are nearly always heredocs: the code looks like the message it prints.

examples.title: Generate a config file
examples.prompt: Write an nginx server block into `site.conf` from three variables, then print the file.
examples.explanation: `cat > site.conf <<EOF` sends the heredoc to `cat`, and `cat`'s output into the file, so `site.conf` holds the text with the three variables filled in. nginx has variables of its own that also start with `$`, like `$uri`. Writing them as `\$uri` keeps them literal, while `$port` still expands. Deploy scripts generate configs this way: one template in the script, different values per server.

examples.title: Literal and indented heredocs
examples.prompt: Write a small script with a quoted heredoc so its `$HOME` stays as typed, run it, then print a note from an indented `<<-` heredoc.
examples.code:
cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Hello from $HOME"
EOF

cat hello.sh
bash hello.sh

if [[ -f hello.sh ]]; then
	cat <<-EOF
		hello.sh is ready.
		Run it with: bash hello.sh
	EOF
fi
examples.output:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Hello from $HOME"
Hello from /home/learner
hello.sh is ready.
Run it with: bash hello.sh
examples.explanation: With `<<'EOF'` nothing expands, so `hello.sh` gets `$HOME` exactly as typed, which `cat hello.sh` shows. When `bash hello.sh` runs the new script, its `$HOME` expands to `/home/learner`. The second heredoc uses `<<-EOF`, which removes the leading tabs from each line and from the closing `EOF`, so the block can sit indented inside the `if` and still print flush left. It only works with tabs: an `EOF` indented with spaces isn't the closing line, and Bash reads on to the end of the file looking for one.

practice.title: Generate a unit file
practice.prompt:
Write a systemd unit file from three environment variables: `SERVICE`, `RUN_USER`, and `PORT`. (`USER` already holds your own user name, which is why this one is `RUN_USER`.)

1. Write `app.service` with one heredoc, laid out exactly like the expected output below.
2. Use `$SERVICE` wherever the output shows `shopfront`, `$RUN_USER` for `deploy`, and `$PORT` for `8080`.
3. Print the file with `cat`.

Test 1 runs with `SERVICE=shopfront`, `RUN_USER=deploy`, and `PORT=8080`, and test 2 with other values. Check compares what you print and what `app.service` holds.

Expected output:

```text
[Unit]
Description=shopfront service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=deploy
ExecStart=/srv/shopfront/bin/server --port 8080
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```
practice.starter:
# Writes a systemd unit for $SERVICE, run by $RUN_USER, on port $PORT.
# TODO: finish the heredoc: add the [Service] and [Install] sections
# TODO: and put the three variables where the values change
cat > app.service <<EOF
[Unit]
Description=my service
EOF

cat app.service
practice.solution:
cat > app.service <<EOF
[Unit]
Description=$SERVICE service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=$RUN_USER
ExecStart=/srv/$SERVICE/bin/server --port $PORT
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

cat app.service

tests.output:
[Unit]
Description=shopfront service
After=network.target

[Service]
User=deploy
ExecStart=/srv/shopfront/bin/server --port 8080
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

tests.output:

hints: Follow the example that writes `site.conf`: `cat > app.service <<EOF`, the lines, `EOF`, then `cat app.service`.
Leave the word unquoted, `<<EOF` and not `<<'EOF'`, or the file gets `$SERVICE` as typed instead of its value.
The line with two variables is `ExecStart=/srv/$SERVICE/bin/server --port $PORT`.

steps.title: Here strings and grouped output
steps.body:
A here string, `<<<`, feeds one string to a command's stdin, with a newline added at the end:

```bash
line="ada devbox 22"
read -r user host port <<< "$line"
echo "$user on $host, port $port"
```

It looks like `echo "$line" | read -r user host port`, but that version doesn't work. Each command in a pipeline runs in a subshell, so `read` sets the variables in a copy of your shell that ends right away. A here string runs `read` in your shell. Quote the string, `<<< "$line"`, so it arrives exactly as stored.

To send the output of several commands to one file, group them with braces and redirect the group once:

```bash
{ echo "# Report"; date -u -d @0; echo "rows: 3"; } > report.md
cat report.md
```

The braces need a space after `{` and a `;` or a line break before `}`. The file is opened once for the whole group, so you don't repeat `>> report.md` on every line.

examples.title: Split a string
examples.prompt: Split strings into variables with `read` and a here string, including a line taken from `config.ini`.
examples.code:
read -r user host <<< "ada devbox"
echo "user: $user"
echo "host: $host"

IFS=: read -r key value <<< "port:8080"
echo "$key is $value"

IFS='=' read -r key value <<< "$(grep '^target=' config.ini)"
echo "$key is $value"
examples.output:
user: ada
host: devbox
port is 8080
target is release
examples.explanation: `read` splits its line on spaces, so `ada` lands in `user` and `devbox` in `host`. `IFS=:` in front of `read` splits on the colon instead, for that one command only, and `IFS='='` splits a `key=value` line. The last here string holds a command substitution: `grep` finds the `target=` line in `config.ini`, and `read` splits it. `read` runs in your shell, not in a pipeline's subshell, so the variables are still set on the next line.

examples.title: Count text in a variable
examples.prompt: Count the words and the matching lines in text that's already in a variable.
examples.code:
sentence="the deploy moves to Thursday"
echo "words: $(wc -w <<< "$sentence")"

output=$(printf '%s\n' "web-1 ok" "web-2 ok" "db-1 timeout" "cache-1 ok")
echo "healthy: $(grep -c ok <<< "$output")"
echo "problems: $(grep -v ok <<< "$output")"
examples.explanation: `wc` and `grep` read stdin when you name no file, and a here string is stdin, so you can count text that never touched a file. `wc -w` counts the 5 words of `sentence`. `output` holds four lines, and the here string passes them on with their line breaks, so `grep -c ok` counts 3 lines and `grep -v ok` prints the one without `ok`. This is how a script looks at a command's captured output several times without running the command again.

examples.title: One redirect for many lines
examples.prompt: Build `inventory.txt` from a heredoc header and a loop over `hosts.txt`, with one redirect for the whole group.
examples.code:
{
  cat <<EOF
# Inventory, generated by $0
# $(wc -l < hosts.txt) hosts
EOF
  while IFS= read -r host; do
    printf '%-10s %s\n' "$host" "${host%-*}"
  done < hosts.txt
} > inventory.txt

cat inventory.txt
examples.output:
# Inventory, generated by main.sh
# 5 hosts
web-1      web
web-2      web
db-1       db
cache-1    cache
backup-1   backup
examples.explanation: Everything between `{` and `}` goes to `inventory.txt`: first the heredoc's two comment lines, then one line per host from the loop. `%-10s` pads each name to 10 characters, and `${host%-*}` cuts the `-1` off the end to get the role. The loop reads `hosts.txt` through its own `<`, and the group's `>` decides where all the output goes. The closing `EOF` still sits alone at the start of its line, even inside the braces. Without the braces you'd write `>` on the first command and `>>` on the others, and one wrong `>` would wipe what came before.

practice.title: Hosts file
practice.prompt:
Turn `NAME IP` lines from stdin into a hosts file.

1. Send everything below into `hosts.out` with one redirect on a `{ ...; }` group.
2. Inside the group, start with a heredoc that writes the two header lines shown below. The first one names the script with `$0`.
3. Then read each `NAME IP` line and write it with `printf '%-15s %s\n' "$ip" "$name"`.
4. After the group, print `hosts.out` with `cat`.

Check compares what you print and what `hosts.out` holds, for two lists of hosts.

Input:

```text
web-1 10.0.0.11
web-2 10.0.0.12
db-1 10.0.0.21
```

Expected output:

```text
# Generated by main.sh from stdin. Do not edit.
127.0.0.1       localhost
10.0.0.11       web-1
10.0.0.12       web-2
10.0.0.21       db-1
```
practice.starter:
# Builds hosts.out from NAME IP lines on stdin.
# TODO: write the two header lines with a heredoc before the loop,
# TODO: send both to hosts.out with one { ...; } group, then print it
while read -r name ip; do
  printf '%-15s %s\n' "$ip" "$name"
done
practice.solution:
{
  cat <<EOF
# Generated by $0 from stdin. Do not edit.
127.0.0.1       localhost
EOF
  while read -r name ip; do
    printf '%-15s %s\n' "$ip" "$name"
  done
} > hosts.out

cat hosts.out

tests.output:
# Generated by main.sh from stdin. Do not edit.
127.0.0.1       localhost
10.0.0.11       web-1
10.0.0.12       web-2
10.0.0.21       db-1

hints: Start from the inventory example: a heredoc and a loop inside `{` and `}`, and `> hosts.out` after the closing brace.
Copy the `127.0.0.1` line from the expected output into the heredoc as it is. Leave the heredoc's word unquoted so `$0` expands.
The shape is `{`, then `cat <<EOF`, the two header lines, `EOF`, the `while read -r name ip` loop, `} > hosts.out`, and finally `cat hosts.out`.

recap:
- `cmd <<EOF` feeds the lines up to `EOF` to a command's stdin, with variables and `$(...)` expanded.
- `<<'EOF'` keeps the text literal, and `\$` gives one literal `$` in an unquoted heredoc.
- `cat > file <<EOF` writes a file from a template in your script.
- `<<-EOF` removes leading tabs, so a heredoc can be indented with tabs.
- `cmd <<< "$var"` feeds one string to a command, and `read -r a b <<< "$line"` splits it in your own shell.
- `{ cmd1; cmd2; } > file` sends the output of a whole group to one file.
